components.text: The decisive demand is whether the proposed evidentiary facts are sufficiently secure to anchor explanation.
The burial argument depends on early independent and reliable traditions.
The empty-tomb argument depends on early independent and reliable traditions.
The appearance evidence depends partly on the reliability and interpretation of transmitted accounts.
Whether the evidentiary facts are sufficiently agreed and securely sourced to anchor the proposed explanatory comparison.
Whether the burial traditions are early, independent, and reliable enough to establish Joseph's identifiable tomb.
Whether the Gospel traditions reliably and independently establish discovery of an empty tomb by women.
Whether late interested narrative sources reliably establish the detailed appearance reports.
The decisive demand is whether resurrection may rank as historically probable under historical explanatory criteria.
Whether ordinary historical comparison can rank a divine miracle as the most probable explanation.
Whether separating facts from explanation makes supernatural causation historically admissible.
The decisive demand is whether low intrinsic probability alone precludes a probable resurrection conclusion.
Whether low intrinsic probability alone determines the posterior historical probability of resurrection.
The decisive demand is whether Gospel imperfections and inconsistencies defeat the reliability of the core facts.
Ideal source criteria must be applied realistically to ancient evidence rather than as absolute prerequisites.
Whether Gospel imperfections and inconsistencies defeat their use for the four asserted central facts.
Whether ancient evidence must satisfy an ideal abundance-and-independence standard before supporting central historical conclusions.
The decisive demand is whether early independent evidence specifically attests burial by Joseph of Arimathea.
The reply asks whether later embellished details are historical under the proposed central-agreement standard.
Whether Paul and the earliest sources specifically attest burial by Joseph of Arimathea.
Whether privileging sparse early agreement while discounting later embellishment applies a consistent historical standard.
The decisive demand is whether inventing women as witnesses would have been too awkward to serve Christian purposes.
The Joseph tradition is also defended by an asserted lack of plausible Christian invention motive.
Whether inventing women as tomb discoverers would be too awkward to serve Christian literary purposes.
Whether Joseph's role would have been unlikely to be invented by Christians.
The decisive demand is whether appearance reports specifically support a bodily resurrection rather than visions.
The comparative inference requires connecting appearance evidence to the proposed bodily and divine explanation.
Whether reports of postmortem appearances establish bodily resurrection rather than visionary or transformed-body experiences.
Whether narrated extraordinary bodily properties can be established as a historical rather than theological conclusion.
The decisive demand is whether historical inquiry may infer a cause that is not directly observable.
The reply also challenges the claim that lack of direct access bars historical inference to resurrection.
Whether lack of direct access to divine action makes resurrection categorically unavailable to historical inference.
Whether extraordinary or inaccessible causal claims are thereby theological rather than historically inferable.
The decisive demand is whether indirect inference suffices when the proposed cause presupposes disputed theology.
Conditional comparison requires priors and likelihoods that historians of divergent worldviews can share.
Whether indirect inference alone makes divine resurrection available under shared historical standards.
Whether a probability framework can yield shared conclusions when its theological priors materially diverge.
Whether resurrection's comparative plausibility depends on prior theistic commitments.
The decisive demand is whether resurrection explains the aftermath better than available ordinary alternatives.
The alternative disputes whether Joseph's identifiable burial is historically established.
The alternative disputes whether an empty tomb is independently established.
The alternative interprets appearances as visions rather than bodily encounters.
Whether resurrection is superior to an ordinary removal-plus-visions account of the disputed aftermath.
Whether burial by Joseph is sufficiently established to constrain body-removal scenarios.
Whether an empty tomb is sufficiently established rather than a later tradition.
Whether appearance reports are equally compatible with visions.
Whether sincere belief and disputed martyrdom claims require bodily resurrection.
The decisive demand is how sincere resurrection belief could arise despite contrary prior expectations.
The account interprets later experiences as visions shaped by an already developing exaltation belief.
Whether sincere resurrection belief requires immediate bodily encounters rather than a developmental causal pathway.
Whether visions could arise after scriptural reinterpretation and reinforce resurrection belief.
Whether a developmental account reduces the need for bodily resurrection as a unified explanation.
The decisive demand is whether historical criteria uniquely prefer the Christian divine-resurrection explanation.
Indirect inference alone does not supply criteria for selecting among rival supernatural agents or purposes.
Whether historical criteria uniquely select the Christian resurrection account over rival supernatural explanations.
Whether inferability of inaccessible events supplies historical criteria for choosing among rival divine causes.
The decisive demand is whether rival theological explanations can be comparatively assessed rather than declared historically tied.
The reply proposes explanatory criteria and context as publicly discussable comparative considerations.
Whether rival theological explanations are immune from comparative explanatory assessment.
Whether public explanatory criteria can assess theological hypotheses despite differing worldview commitments.
